meta.spelling: Modern spelling text as published by the Orthodox Presbyterian Church.
meta.proofs: Scripture proof citations are from the Orthodox Presbyterian Church editions with proof texts: https://opc.org/documents/CFLayout.pdf, https://opc.org/documents/SCLayout.pdf, and https://opc.org/documents/LCLayout.pdf. The Standards themselves use the constitutional text published by the OPC.

wcf-7-3.heading: Of God’s Covenant with Man
wcf-7-3.text: 3. Man, by his fall, having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace; wherein he freely offereth unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ; requiring of them faith in him, that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal life his Holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe.
wcf-7-3.proofs: Galatians 3:21; Romans 3:20-21; Romans 8:3; Genesis 3:15; Isaiah 42:6; John 3:16; Romans 10:6, 9; Revelation 22:17; Acts 13:48; Ezekiel 36:26-27; John 6:37, 44-45; 1 Corinthians 12:3

wcf-7-5.heading: Of God’s Covenant with Man
wcf-7-5.text: 5. This covenant was differently administered in the time of the law, and in the time of the gospel: under the law, it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances delivered to the people of the Jews, all foresignifying Christ to come; which were, for that time, sufficient and efficacious, through the operation of the Spirit, to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, by whom they had full remission of sins, and eternal salvation; and is called the old testament.
wcf-7-5.proofs: 2 Corinthians 3:6-9; Hebrews 8-10; Romans 4:11; Colossians 2:11-12; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Corinthians 10:1-4; Hebrews 11:13; John 8:56; Galatians 3:7-9, 14; Psalm 32:1-2, 5

wcf-7-6.heading: Of God’s Covenant with Man
wcf-7-6.text: 6. Under the gospel, when Christ, the substance, was exhibited, the ordinances in which this covenant is dispensed are the preaching of the Word, and the administration of the sacraments of baptism and the Lord’s Supper: which, though fewer in number, and administered with more simplicity, and less outward glory, yet, in them, it is held forth in more fullness, evidence and spiritual efficacy, to all nations, both Jews and Gentiles; and is called the new testament. There are not therefore two covenants of grace, differing in substance, but one and the same, under various dispensations.
wcf-7-6.proofs: Colossians 2:17; 1 Corinthians 1:21; Matthew 28:19-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-25; Hebrews 12:22-24; 2 Corinthians 3:9-11; Jeremiah 31:33-34; Luke 2:32; Acts 10:34; Ephesians 2:15-19; Luke 22:20; Galatians 3:8-9, 14, 16; Romans 3:21-22, 30; Romans 4:3, 6-8, 16-17, 23-24; Genesis 15:6; Psalm 32:1-2; Hebrews 4:2; Romans 10:6-10; 1 Corinthians 10:3-4

wcf-8-1.heading: Of Christ the Mediator
wcf-8-1.text: 1. It pleased God, in his eternal purpose, to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, his only begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man, the Prophet, Priest, and King, the Head and Savior of his church, the Heir of all things, and Judge of the world: unto whom he did from all eternity give a people, to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified.
wcf-8-1.proofs: Isaiah 42:1; 1 Peter 1:19-20; John 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:5; Acts 3:20, 22; Deuteronomy 18:15; Hebrews 5:5-6; Psalm 2:6; Luke 1:33; Isaiah 9:5-6; Acts 2:29-36; Colossians 1:13; Ephesians 5:23; Hebrews 1:2; Acts 17:31; John 17:6; Psalm 22:30; Isaiah 53:10; Ephesians 1:4; 1 Timothy 2:6; Isaiah 55:4-5; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Romans 8:30

wcf-8-2.heading: Of Christ the Mediator
wcf-8-2.text: 2. The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father, did, when the fullness of time was come, take upon him man’s nature, with all the essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin; being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the virgin Mary, of her substance. So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. Which person is very God, and very man, yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and man.
wcf-8-2.proofs: John 1:1, 14; 1 John 5:20; Philippians 2:6; Galatians 4:4; Philippians 2:7; Hebrews 2:14, 16-17; Hebrews 4:15; Luke 1:27, 31, 35; Matthew 1:18, 20-21; Matthew 16:16; Colossians 2:9; Romans 9:5; 1 Timothy 3:16; Romans 1:3-4; 1 Timothy 2:5

wcf-8-6.heading: Of Christ the Mediator
wcf-8-6.text: 6. Although the work of redemption was not actually wrought by Christ till after his incarnation, yet the virtue, efficacy, and benefits thereof were communicated unto the elect, in all ages successively from the beginning of the world, in and by those promises, types, and sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the seed of the woman which should bruise the serpent’s head; and the Lamb slain from the beginning of the world; being yesterday and today the same, and forever.
wcf-8-6.proofs: Galatians 4:4-5; Genesis 3:15; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Revelation 13:8; Hebrews 13:8; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 9:15

wsc-20.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-20.text:
Q. 20. Did God leave all mankind to perish in the estate of sin and misery?
A. God having, out of his mere good pleasure, from all eternity, elected some to everlasting life, did enter into a covenant of grace, to deliver them out of the estate of sin and misery, and to bring them into an estate of salvation by a redeemer.
wsc-20.proofs: Acts 13:48; Ephesians 1:4-5; 2 Thessalonians 2:13-14; Genesis 3:15; Genesis 17:7; Exodus 19:5-6; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Matthew 20:28; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Hebrews 9:15

wsc-21.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-21.text:
Q. 21. Who is the redeemer of God’s elect?
A. The only redeemer of God’s elect is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, became man, and so was, and continueth to be, God and man in two distinct natures, and one person, forever.
wsc-21.proofs: John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5-6; Psalm 2:7; Matthew 3:17; Matthew 17:5; John 1:18; Isaiah 9:6; Matthew 1:23; John 1:14; Galatians 4:4; Acts 1:11; Hebrews 7:24-25

wsc-22.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-22.text:
Q. 22. How did Christ, being the Son of God, become man?
A. Christ, the Son of God, became man, by taking to himself a true body and a reasonable soul, being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the virgin Mary, and born of her, yet without sin.
wsc-22.proofs: Philippians 2:7; Hebrews 2:14, 17; Luke 1:27, 31, 35; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; Hebrews 7:26; 1 John 3:5

wsc-23.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-23.text:
Q. 23. What offices doth Christ execute as our redeemer?
A. Christ, as our redeemer, executeth the offices of a prophet, of a priest, and of a king, both in his estate of humiliation and exaltation.
wsc-23.proofs: Deuteronomy 18:18; Acts 2:33; Acts 3:22-23; Hebrews 1:1-2; Hebrews 4:14-15; Hebrews 5:5-6; Isaiah 9:6-7; Luke 1:32-33; John 18:37; 1 Corinthians 15:25

wsc-26.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-26.text:
Q. 26. How doth Christ execute the office of a king?
A. Christ executeth the office of a king, in subduing us to himself, in ruling and defending us, and in restraining and conquering all his and our enemies.
wsc-26.proofs: Psalm 110:3; Matthew 28:18-20; John 17:2; Colossians 1:13; Psalm 2:6-9; Psalm 110:1-2; Matthew 12:28; 1 Corinthians 15:24-26; Colossians 2:15

wsc-27.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-27.text:
Q. 27. Wherein did Christ’s humiliation consist?
A. Christ’s humiliation consisted in his being born, and that in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; in being buried, and continuing under the power of death for a time.
wsc-27.proofs: Luke 2:7; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Galatians 4:4; Isaiah 53:3; Luke 9:58; John 4:6; John 11:35; Hebrews 2:18; Psalm 22:1; Matthew 27:46; Isaiah 53:10; 1 John 2:2; Galatians 3:13; Philippians 2:8; Matthew 12:40; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4

wsc-86.heading: Westminster Shorter Catechism
wsc-86.text:
Q. 86. What is faith in Jesus Christ?
A. Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel.

wlc-36.heading: Westminster Larger Catechism
wlc-36.text:
Q. 36. Who is the mediator of the covenant of grace?
A. The only mediator of the covenant of grace is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, of one substance and equal with the Father, in the fullness of time became man, and so was and continues to be God and man, in two entire distinct natures, and one person, forever.
wlc-36.proofs: 1 Timothy 2:5; John 14:6; Acts 4:12; John 1:1, 14, 18; John 10:30; Philippians 2:6; Psalm 2:7; Matthew 3:17; Matthew 17:5; Galatians 4:4; Matthew 1:23; Luke 1:35; Acts 1:11; Romans 9:5; Colossians 2:9; Hebrews 7:24-25; Hebrews 13:8; Philippians 2:5-11

wlc-41.heading: Westminster Larger Catechism
wlc-41.text:
Q. 41. Why was our mediator called Jesus?
A. Our mediator was called Jesus, because he saveth his people from their sins.

wlc-42.heading: Westminster Larger Catechism
wlc-42.text:
Q. 42. Why was our mediator called Christ?
A. Our mediator was called Christ, because he was anointed with the Holy Ghost above measure; and so set apart, and fully furnished with all authority and ability, to execute the offices of prophet, priest, and king of his church, in the estate both of his humiliation and exaltation.
wlc-42.proofs: Matthew 3:16; Acts 10:37-38; John 3:34; Psalm 45:7; John 6:27; Matthew 28:18-20; Romans 1:3-4; Acts 3:21-22; Luke 4:18, 21; Hebrews 1:1-2; Deuteronomy 18:18; Hebrews 5:5-7; Hebrews 4:14-15; Psalm 2:6; Luke 1:32-34; John 18:37; Matthew 21:5; Isaiah 9:6-7; Philippians 2:8-11

wlc-47.heading: Westminster Larger Catechism
wlc-47.text:
Q. 47. How did Christ humble himself in his conception and birth?
A. Christ humbled himself in his conception and birth, in that, being from all eternity the Son of God, in the bosom of the Father, he was pleased in the fullness of time to become the son of man, made of a woman of low estate, and to be born of her; with divers circumstances of more than ordinary abasement.

promise_seed.line: The confession reads this promise as being about Jesus. Long before he was born, God was already pointing to the child who would crush the serpent.
promise_seed.explain: This paragraph teaches that Christ's saving work reached God's people even before Bethlehem. God showed him in promises, pictures, and sacrifices. The seed of the woman who bruises the serpent's head is named as one of those signs. That is this node's verse, read as a word about Christ. Genesis 3:15 and Galatians 4:4-5 are both among the printed proofs.

promise_seed.line: A covenant of grace is the binding relationship God establishes to offer sinners life and salvation through Jesus Christ.
promise_seed.explain: This paragraph teaches why the covenant of grace was needed. People could not earn life after the fall. God freely offers life and salvation through Jesus Christ and promises the Spirit to those he will save. The printed proofs include Genesis 3:15, Galatians 3:21, John 3:16, and John 6:37, 44-45.

promise_seed.line: God did not leave all mankind to perish. He covenanted to save his elect through a redeemer.
promise_seed.explain: The question asks if God left all mankind to perish. The answer is no. From his own pleasure he elected some to everlasting life and made a covenant of grace to save through a redeemer. The proofs include Acts 13:48, Ephesians 1:4-5, Genesis 3:15, and Hebrews 9:15.

promise_abraham.line: Before Jesus came, God taught this same promise with words, worship, and pictures. A type is a picture God gave ahead of time. It was meant to point to Jesus.
promise_abraham.explain: Before Christ came, the same covenant was handed on by promises, prophecies, and worship that pointed forward. The proofs include John 8:56, Abraham rejoicing to see Christ's day, and Galatians 3:7-9 and 14, the blessing of Abraham coming to the nations in Christ.

promise_abraham.line: The promise did not turn into a different plan when Jesus arrived. He is the real thing those earlier words were about, for every nation.
promise_abraham.explain: Christ is the substance, the reality the signs were about. There are not two covenants of grace. Galatians 3:16 is in the proof list, the verse that says the offspring is Christ. Abraham's promise and Jesus are one plan.

promise_judah.line: Judah's family was promised a ruler. The catechism says Jesus is king: he rules his people and overcomes his enemies.
promise_judah.explain: Christ's kingship is not a metaphor only. He subdues a people to himself, rules and defends them, and conquers his enemies. Judah's scepter is the family form of that office. Psalms 2 and 110 are among the printed proofs.

promise_judah.line: Christ means the anointed one, the person God set apart as prophet, priest, and king. That is the ruler Judah was promised.
promise_judah.explain: Christ means anointed. He was set apart by the Holy Spirit to be prophet, priest, and king. A scepter promise needs that title, or it shrinks into politics. Isaiah 9:6-7 is printed with this answer.

jesse_root.line: Isaiah saw a new king growing from Jesse's family, like a shoot from an old stump. Christ means the one God anointed for that work.
jesse_root.explain: The branch from Jesse bears the Spirit and judges the earth. The catechism's word for that person is Christ, the anointed king, prophet, and priest. The family stump and the anointing belong together.

covenant_david.line: God told David that his son would reign forever. The catechism says Jesus is the king who defends his people.
covenant_david.explain: The son on David's throne reigns as Christ reigns in this answer: ruling, defending, and conquering. The angel will put that reign on Jesus. Psalms 2 and 110 are among the printed proofs.

prophecy_immanuel.line: Immanuel means God with us. The confession says Jesus is truly God and truly human, conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit.
prophecy_immanuel.explain: The Son took a true human nature, conceived by the Holy Spirit in the virgin Mary, and is one person, truly God and truly man. That is Immanuel as doctrine. Luke 1:27, 31, and 35, and Galatians 4:4, are proofs.

prophecy_immanuel.line: In fewer words, Jesus took a real body and a real human soul. He was born of Mary, and he was without sin.
prophecy_immanuel.explain: The shorter answer says he took a true body and a reasonable soul, was conceived by the Spirit, and was born of Mary without sin. God with us is God become man, not God standing at a distance.

prophecy_child.line: Isaiah says a child will be born who carries the government on his shoulder. The catechism says Jesus serves us as prophet, priest, and king.
prophecy_child.explain: The child with the government on his shoulder is described here as prophet, priest, and king. Isaiah 9:6-7 is one of the proofs attached to this answer. The names in Isaiah and the offices in the catechism are meant to be read together.

bethlehem.line: Jesus was born in humble circumstances. The catechism says his humiliation included being born in a low condition.
bethlehem.explain: Humiliation includes being born in a low condition. Luke 2:7 is the first proof. The catechism does not make Bethlehem's size or name part of the doctrine.

bethlehem.line: His birth came with circumstances of unusual humility.
bethlehem.explain: The answer stays on conception and birth. The proofs name John 1:14, 18, Galatians 4:4, and Luke 2:7.

mary.line: Mary is the virgin in this paragraph. Jesus was conceived in her by the Holy Spirit, and he is God and man in one person.
mary.explain: Mary is named. The Son's human nature is from her, by the Holy Spirit, without sin. She is the mother of the incarnation, not a second mediator. Luke 1:27, 31, and 35 are proofs.

mary.line: He took a real human body and soul, was born of Mary, and was without sin.
mary.explain: Born of her, yet without sin, is the catechism's sentence for Mary's child. The body and the soul are real. The conception is the Spirit's work.

annunciation.line: Gabriel told Mary she would conceive by the Holy Spirit. That is what the confession teaches about how Jesus became man.
annunciation.explain: Gabriel tells Mary what this paragraph teaches. The Spirit will overshadow her. The child will be holy. The confession adds that the one person is truly God and truly man. The annunciation verses are proofs.

annunciation.line: Gabriel also said her son would have David's throne. The catechism says Jesus really is king.
annunciation.explain: The throne of David in the angel's speech is kingship. This answer says Christ rules and defends his people and conquers his enemies. The announcement is about a king, not only a miracle.

jesus_birth.line: Jesus was born as a real baby, with a real body, and he was without sin.
jesus_birth.explain: The manger holds a true body. The catechism insists on a true body and a reasonable soul, born of Mary without sin. Christmas is not God visiting in disguise.

jesus_birth.line: The eternal Son of God chose a humble birth. The manger is part of that lowliness.
jesus_birth.explain: The same night is humiliation. The Son became man in low estate, with humble circumstances. Luke 2:7, the proof, records the manger because there was no place in the inn.

jesus.line: A mediator stands between God and us. Jesus is that person. He is prophet, priest, and king, and he saves his people.
jesus.explain: God ordained his Son to be mediator, prophet, priest, and king, and gave him a people. Matthew's first verse presents that person as son of David and son of Abraham. Luke 1:33 is a proof for the throne.

jesus.line: Jesus is fully God and fully human, one person, forever. He is the only rescuer of God's people.
jesus.explain: There is one redeemer. He became man and remains God and man forever. The proofs include John 1:14, Galatians 4:4, and Matthew 1:23, the verses of his coming in the flesh.

jesus.line: The one promise that runs through the Bible has one mediator. A mediator is the person who brings God and people together. That person is Jesus.
jesus.explain: He is the only mediator of the covenant of grace. The many promises on the map do not mean many saviors. The proofs repeat Luke 1:35, Galatians 4:4, and 1 Timothy 2:5.

jesus.line: Matthew connects Jesus' name with his work: he saves his people from their sins.
jesus.explain: Matthew 1:21 gives the name and then explains Jesus' saving work. This is the passage's own wordplay, not a complete dictionary definition of the name.

magi.line: They came looking for a king. The catechism says Christ rules and defends his people and conquers his enemies.
magi.explain: They call the child king and worship him. The catechism explains Christ's kingly office. Their gifts do not prove any separate doctrine.

bread_of_life.line: When Jesus says he is the bread of life, he means people truly live by trusting him. The catechism calls that trust faith. We rest on him alone to save us.
bread_of_life.explain: Faith receives Christ and rests on him alone. Jesus says the bread of life is himself, received by coming and believing. This catechism answer does not cite John 6. It cites Ephesians 2:8-9, John 20:30-31, Galatians 2:15-16, and Philippians 3:3-11. Do not turn the Bethlehem wordplay into this doctrine.

dt_moses.line: The confession reads the whole law given through Moses as one administration of the covenant of grace, pointing forward to Christ.
dt_moses.explain: This paragraph says that before Christ came, the same covenant of grace was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, and other types and ordinances given to the people of the Jews, all foresignifying Christ to come. Deuteronomy is Moses explaining that body of law to Israel. The confession does not claim that any particular verse of Deuteronomy names Christ. It claims that the arrangement as a whole pointed to him.

dt_prophet.line: The catechism lists the office of prophet among the offices Christ was anointed to hold, and prints this Deuteronomy verse among its proofs.
dt_prophet.explain: The answer explains why our mediator is called Christ: he was anointed and set apart to execute the offices of prophet, priest, and king. Deuteronomy 18:18, the promise read at this stop, is one of the Scripture proofs printed with the answer, alongside Acts 3:21-22. So the identification of the promised prophet with Christ is the confessional reading, and the Standards cite this verse for it.

dt_hanged.line: The catechism includes the cursed death of the cross in its account of Christ's humiliation, and prints Paul's use of this verse among its proofs.
dt_hanged.explain: The answer describes Christ's humiliation as his being born in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross. Galatians 3:13, where Paul quotes this Deuteronomy law, is one of the proofs printed with the answer. Deuteronomy itself is giving a burial rule. The confessional claim rests on Paul's use of it.

nt_acts3.line: Peter's sermon is one of the proofs the catechism prints for Christ holding the office of prophet.
nt_acts3.explain: The answer says Christ was set apart and furnished to execute the offices of prophet, priest, and king. Acts 3:21-22, the passage at this stop, is printed among its Scripture proofs, together with Deuteronomy 18:18. The catechism is reading Peter's sermon the same way Peter does, as naming Jesus the prophet Moses promised.

nt_gal3.line: The verse at this stop is one of the proofs printed with the catechism's answer on Christ's humiliation.
nt_gal3.explain: The answer names the cursed death of the cross as part of what Christ's humiliation consisted in, and Galatians 3:13 is among the Scripture proofs listed with it. Paul's sentence, that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, is the text the Standards lean on at that point.

nt_rom10.line: The confession teaches that there is one covenant of grace under two administrations, and prints this passage among its proofs.
nt_rom10.explain: The paragraph says the ordinances under the gospel are fewer and simpler but hold the same covenant forth more fully, and that there are not two covenants of grace differing in substance but one and the same under various dispensations. Romans 10:6-10 is among the Scripture proofs printed with it. That is why a Reformed reader is unsurprised to find Paul taking words Moses spoke about the commandment and applying them to the gospel.

is_child.line: The catechism prints this passage among its proofs for the offices of Christ.
is_child.explain: The answer says that Christ, as our redeemer, executes the offices of a prophet, a priest, and a king. Isaiah 9:6-7, the child with the government on his shoulder and the throne of David, is one of the Scripture proofs listed with it, beside Luke 1:32-33.

is_servant_chosen.line: The confession begins its chapter on Christ the Mediator with God choosing him, and this verse is its first proof.
is_servant_chosen.explain: The paragraph says it pleased God, in his eternal purpose, to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus to be the Mediator between God and man. Isaiah 42:1, 'Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen', is the first Scripture proof printed with it.

is_servant_suffering.line: Two verses from this chapter are among the proofs printed with the catechism's answer on Christ's humiliation.
is_servant_suffering.explain: The answer lists what Christ's humiliation consisted in: the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross. Isaiah 53:3, the man of sorrows, and Isaiah 53:10, the LORD's will to crush him, are both among its Scripture proofs.

is_anointed.line: The catechism explains the name Christ by his anointing with the Holy Spirit, and it cites the scene where Jesus reads this passage.
is_anointed.explain: The answer says our mediator was called Christ because he was anointed with the Holy Ghost above measure, and so set apart to be prophet, priest, and king. Luke 4:18 and 21, where Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and says it is fulfilled, are among the proofs printed with it. Isaiah 61 itself is not in the list. The proof is Luke's account of Jesus reading it.

isn_lk4.line: The verses at this stop are among the proofs printed with the catechism's answer on why the mediator is called Christ.
isn_lk4.explain: The answer says he was anointed with the Holy Ghost above measure and fully furnished to execute the offices of prophet, priest, and king. Luke 4:18 and 21 are listed with it. Jesus reads that the Spirit of the Lord is upon him and says the Scripture is fulfilled.

isn_mt1.line: The verse Matthew quotes here is among the proofs printed with the catechism's answer on who the redeemer is.
isn_mt1.explain: The answer says the only redeemer of God's elect is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, became man. Matthew 1:23, Immanuel, God with us, is one of the Scripture proofs listed with it.

rvo_seed.line: The confession calls Christ the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head.
rvo_seed.explain: This paragraph says that the benefits of Christ's redemption were communicated to the elect in all ages from the beginning of the world, in and by the promises, types, and sacrifices in which he was revealed and signified to be the seed of the woman. Genesis 3:15 is printed among its Scripture proofs. So is Revelation 13:8, the Lamb who was slain.

rvo_passover.line: The confession names the paschal lamb among the things that pointed forward to Christ.
rvo_passover.explain: This paragraph says the covenant of grace was administered under the law by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances, all foresignifying Christ to come. Paschal means of the Passover. 1 Corinthians 5:7, where Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb, is among the proofs printed with it.

rv_dragon.line: The confession speaks of the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head, and of the Lamb slain from the beginning of the world.
rv_dragon.explain: The paragraph teaches that Christ's work, though done in time, has saved God's people in every age. Its Scripture proofs include Genesis 3:15 and Revelation 13:8. Revelation 12 shows the serpent, the woman's child, and the victory won by the blood of the Lamb. The confession does not cite Revelation 12 itself.

rv_river.line: A verse from this chapter is among the proofs printed with the confession's paragraph on the covenant of grace.
rv_river.explain: The paragraph says that in the covenant of grace God freely offers to sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ. Revelation 22:17, the invitation to take the water of life without price, is one of the Scripture proofs listed with it.

week1_seed.line: This week follows one promise as it gets clearer, from the garden, to Abraham, to Jesus. The confession says there are not two different rescue plans. Jesus is the heart of the same promise.
week1_seed.explain: The week is one covenant getting clearer, from the garden to Abraham to the birth. Christ is the substance. Galatians 3:16 is in the proofs. There are not two rescue plans.

week2_king.line: This week follows the promise of a king from David's family. The catechism says Jesus is that king, and also a prophet and a priest.
week2_king.explain: The week follows a king through a family and an announcement. The catechism will not let him be king only. He is also prophet and priest. Isaiah 9:6-7 is a proof of this answer.

week3_sign.line: This week is about the sign of a son born to a virgin. The confession says that son is God with us.
week3_sign.explain: Sign, mother, dream, and birth are the incarnation. The proofs listed with this paragraph include Luke 1 and Galatians 4:4, the week's own texts.

week4_town.line: This week ends in a small town. Jesus chose a humble birth on purpose.
week4_town.explain: Prophet, town, seekers, and manger are the humble birth. The catechism says the Son took that low place on purpose. Luke 2:7 and Galatians 4:4 are the proofs.

christmas.line: Christmas is the birth of the rescuer. He is God and man in one person, forever.
christmas.explain: The night names the redeemer, God and man in one person. The proofs include Matthew 1:23 and Galatians 4:4.

christmas.line: The angel calls him Savior. Matthew connects the name Jesus with saving his people from their sins.
christmas.explain: Luke calls him Savior, and Matthew 1:21 gives his name and explains his saving work. The catechism's proof is Matthew 1:21.

deut_book.line: The confession reads the law given through Moses as one administration of the covenant of grace, sufficient for its time and pointing to Christ.
deut_book.explain: This paragraph is the frame a Reformed reader brings to a walk through Deuteronomy. The promises, prophecies, sacrifices, and ordinances given to Israel were sufficient and effective for that time, through the work of the Spirit, to build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah. The book is not a dead letter and not a finished system. It is one stage of one covenant.

deut_nt.line: The confession says the old and new administrations are not two covenants but one, which is why the apostles can quote Moses as speaking to the church.
deut_nt.explain: The paragraph ends by saying that there are not two covenants of grace differing in substance, but one and the same under various dispensations. Romans 10:6-10, one of the stops on this path, is printed among its proofs. That one covenant is the reason an apostle can take a line from Deuteronomy and address it to readers in Rome or Galatia without arguing that the verse has changed meaning.

isaiah_through.line: The confession says that before Christ came, the covenant of grace was administered by promises and prophecies that pointed to him.
isaiah_through.explain: This paragraph is the frame a Reformed reader brings to Isaiah. Under the law the covenant of grace was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, and other types and ordinances, all foresignifying Christ to come, and these were sufficient for that time to build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah. Isaiah's hearers were saved by trusting the God who made these promises.

isaiah_nt.line: The confession's first paragraph on Christ the Mediator leans on Isaiah three times in its proofs.
isaiah_nt.explain: The paragraph says God chose and ordained the Lord Jesus to be the Mediator, the Prophet, Priest, and King. Among the Scripture proofs printed with it are Isaiah 42:1, Isaiah 53:10, and Isaiah 55:4-5. The Standards read Isaiah the way the New Testament stops on this path do, as speaking of Christ.

rev_ot.line: The confession says the promises, sacrifices, and types of the Old Testament all pointed forward to Christ.
rev_ot.explain: This paragraph is why a Reformed reader expects to find the Old Testament in Revelation. The covenant of grace was administered under the law by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances, all foresignifying Christ to come. John sees the things those pictures pointed to.

nodes.promise_seed: In Reformed theology, Genesis 3:15 is the first gospel promise. Confession 8.6 identifies Christ as the woman's offspring who bruises the serpent's head.
nodes.promise_abraham: Reformed theology reads Abraham's promise within the one covenant of grace. Confession 7.5 and 7.6 say the covenant is one in substance across its different administrations.
nodes.promise_judah: The scepter points to Christ's kingly office. The catechisms describe the Christ as the anointed prophet, priest, and king who rules and defends his people.
nodes.jesse_root: The Spirit resting on Jesse's branch fits the catechism's description of Christ as the one anointed by the Holy Spirit to be prophet, priest, and king.
nodes.covenant_david: The Davidic promise reaches its goal in Christ's kingship. The catechism says he subdues, rules, and defends his people and conquers his enemies.
nodes.prophecy_immanuel: Immanuel is fulfilled in the incarnation. The eternal Son took a true human nature and remains one person with two distinct natures, truly God and truly man.
nodes.prophecy_child: The child on David's throne is read as Christ the king. Shorter Catechism 23 includes Isaiah 9:6-7 among its proofs for Christ's three offices.
nodes.prophecy_bethlehem: The ruler from Bethlehem is read as Christ the king. His place of origin does not make the town itself a saving sign.
nodes.bethlehem: Christ's birth in low circumstances belongs to his humiliation. The catechisms ground that claim in Luke 2:7, not in a symbolic meaning of Bethlehem's name.
nodes.mary: Reformed teaching honors Mary as the virgin mother of Jesus while reserving the work of mediator for Christ alone. The confession says his human nature was conceived in her by the Holy Spirit.
nodes.joseph: Joseph belongs to David's line and names the child, while Scripture says the conception is by the Holy Spirit. The Westminster Standards do not assign Joseph a separate mediatorial role.
nodes.annunciation: The announcement joins incarnation and kingship. The child is conceived by the Holy Spirit and receives David's throne.
nodes.jesus_birth: The birth is both incarnation and humiliation. The eternal Son truly became man and was born in a low condition.
nodes.jesus: Jesus is the only mediator, truly God and truly man, and the anointed prophet, priest, and king.
nodes.magi: The wise men worship the child they call king. Their visit displays his kingship, but the catechisms do not interpret each gift or identify the visitors with a particular prophecy.
nodes.bread_of_life: Coming to Jesus and believing in him is faith, receiving and resting on Christ alone for salvation. This doctrine comes from Jesus' explanation in John 6, not from a wordplay on Bethlehem.
nodes.isaiah: Reformed teaching takes a prophet's words as God's own speech given through a man, so these sentences are Scripture and not religious opinion. Isaiah's part was to speak. What the New Testament announces as fulfillment is God's own work. The God who spoke through Isaiah is the one who brought it about.
nodes.dt_moses: Reformed readers take Deuteronomy as covenant preaching, not as a legal code dropped into the middle of the Bible. Moses is calling a people God already rescued to live as his people in the land he promised. The Confession places the whole arrangement under the covenant of grace, administered for that time by promises, sacrifices, and ordinances that pointed to Christ. Read that way, the book's commands rest on what God has already done.
nodes.dt_decalogue: The Reformed tradition reads the preface to the ten commandments as setting the pattern for all obedience. God names himself as the one who brought Israel out of slavery before he gives a command. Obedience is the response of a people already redeemed, not the price of redemption. The Standards treat the moral law summarized in these commandments as binding on everyone, while denying that keeping it is how anyone is justified.
nodes.dt_shema: Reformed teaching takes this passage as the summary of what God requires in the first table of the law: that he be loved with the whole person. Jesus' use of it settles the matter for Christian readers, since he calls it the great and first commandment. The tradition also notes what the passage assumes, that such love is commanded and not merely invited, which is part of why it teaches that the law shows a reader his need before it shows him his duty.
nodes.dt_wilderness_test: Reformed readers treat the wilderness years as God's fatherly discipline of a people he had already claimed, which is how Deuteronomy 8:5 puts it. The testing is not God finding out what he did not know. It is God exposing what was in Israel's heart, for Israel's sake. Christian readers then set Jesus' forty days beside Israel's forty years. The comparison is an interpretation, and a common one, but Matthew states only the quotation.
nodes.dt_prophet: The Westminster Standards name prophet as one of the three offices Christ holds, and they cite Deuteronomy 18:18 for it. On that reading the promise is not exhausted by Israel's later prophets, though it includes them, because the prophet promised here speaks the words God puts in his mouth with an authority that makes refusal answerable to God. Reformed readers take the apostles' identification of that prophet as Jesus to be the promise's intended end.
nodes.dt_hanged: Reformed theology takes this law as the Old Testament ground for understanding the cross as a curse borne. The law itself is about burial and about keeping the land undefiled. Paul's use of it in Galatians is what makes it doctrine, and the Shorter Catechism follows him by naming the cursed death of the cross in its answer on Christ's humiliation. The tradition is careful here: Deuteronomy supplies the vocabulary of curse, and the apostle supplies the application.
nodes.dt_curses: This passage is central to the Reformed account of what the law does to a sinner. The law promises life to the one who keeps it and pronounces a curse on the one who does not, and the final curse covers the whole law rather than any single command. The tradition concludes that no one is justified by the law, not because the law is faulty, but because the demand is total. That conclusion is Paul's own in Galatians 3.
nodes.dt_word_near: Reformed readers hear this passage as grace inside the law's own sermon. Moses has just finished setting out blessing and curse, and he turns to say that the word is not out of reach. The tradition reads the nearness of the word as God's own doing rather than a comment on human ability, and it points to Paul, who takes the same words and makes them describe the gospel that is preached and believed.
nodes.dt_song: The Song of Moses holds together two things the Reformed tradition insists on keeping together: that God is just in all his ways, and that his people are unfaithful. The song says both in the same breath. It also shows God's purposes reaching past Israel's failure, which Paul takes up in Romans when he quotes verse 21 about a foolish nation. On that reading the song is more than a warning.
nodes.dt_death: Reformed readers note what the book does not do at the end: it does not supply the prophet it promised. Moses dies outside the land, and the last word about him is that no one like him has arisen. Many in the tradition hear the book leaving a space open. That reading is interpretive, and the map marks it dashed, because Deuteronomy says only that no such prophet had arisen, not that one was still to come.
nodes.nt_temptation: Reformed writers have long read the wilderness testing as Christ standing where Adam and Israel fell, and standing by the word of God rather than by raw power. The three answers come from Deuteronomy, which is Israel's own covenant sermon, and that choice is part of the point. The tradition also takes the scene as a defense of Scripture's sufficiency: Jesus meets temptation with it is written.
nodes.nt_greatest: That Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:5 is the warrant for the Reformed treatment of the moral law as a summary of love to God and neighbor. The Standards arrange the commandments under those two heads for exactly this reason. Jesus is not replacing the law with a principle. He is naming what the law was always asking for.
nodes.nt_acts3: Peter's sermon is one of the places the Reformed tradition grounds the prophetic office of Christ, and the Larger Catechism prints it among the proofs. What Reformed readers notice is the shape of the argument. Peter does not invent a meaning for Deuteronomy 18. He quotes it to people who knew it and then says who the prophet is, which is how the apostles read the Old Testament generally.
nodes.nt_gal3: This passage carries a great deal of Reformed doctrine. The law pronounces a curse on everyone who fails to keep it, Christ took that curse in his death, and the blessing promised to Abraham therefore reaches the nations by faith. The Standards follow Paul in naming the cursed death of the cross as part of Christ's humiliation. The tradition also notes that Paul joins two separate Deuteronomy texts to say it, and that the joining is his argument.
nodes.nt_rom10: Reformed readers take Romans 10 as the clearest statement of how the word works: near, preached, heard, believed, confessed. It also shows an apostle handling the Old Testament with freedom and with care at once, reapplying Moses' words about the commandment to the message about Christ. The Confession's teaching that there is one covenant of grace under two administrations is what makes that move intelligible rather than arbitrary, and Romans 10:6-10 is printed among its proofs.
nodes.is_opening: Reformed teaching begins where this chapter begins, with sin as rebellion against the God who made and raised his people. Outward worship does not cover it. The cleansing God offers here is his own gift, and the rest of Isaiah shows that it comes through the servant who bears iniquity.
nodes.is_call: The Reformed tradition returns often to this chapter for the holiness of God. Isaiah's guilt is removed by something done to him from the altar, before he does anything for God. Pardon comes first and service follows. John 12:41 leads Christians to say that the glory Isaiah saw was the glory of Christ.
nodes.is_immanuel: The Standards confess that the eternal Son of God became man, conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary. Matthew 1:23, which quotes this verse, is printed among the proofs of Shorter Catechism 21. Reformed readers take Matthew's use of the verse as settling its final meaning.
nodes.is_child: Shorter Catechism 23 lists Isaiah 9:6-7 among its proofs for the offices of Christ. On the Reformed reading the child on David's throne is Christ the king, and the names Mighty God and Everlasting Father speak of his deity. No New Testament writer quotes verses 6 and 7, so this rests on reading the whole passage together with Matthew 4 and Luke 1.
nodes.is_shoot: The Spirit resting on the shoot from Jesse fits the Larger Catechism's account of why the mediator is called Christ: he was anointed with the Holy Spirit above measure. Paul's quotation of verse 10 in Romans 15:12 is the New Testament warrant for reading this king as Jesus.
nodes.is_babylon: Reformed readers take the fall of Babylon as a lasting pattern as well as a single event. God brings down every power that exalts itself against him, and his people are taught to expect it and to sing about it beforehand. Revelation's use of the name supports reading it that way.
nodes.is_hezekiah: The Shorter Catechism says Christ as king rules and defends his people and restrains and conquers all his and their enemies. Reformed preachers have long used Hezekiah's prayer as a picture of faith under threat: he spreads the matter before the LORD and asks God to act for his own name.
nodes.is_comfort: The comfort announced here rests on pardon. Jerusalem's iniquity is pardoned before any road is built. Reformed theology hears the gospel in that order, and it notes that the way is prepared for the LORD himself, which the Gospels apply to the coming of Jesus.
nodes.is_servant_chosen: Confession 8.1 says it pleased God to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus to be the Mediator, and Isaiah 42:1 is the first Scripture proof printed with it. The Reformed tradition reads God's chosen servant here as Christ, on the authority of Matthew 12:17-21.
nodes.is_cyrus: This passage is a standard text for the Reformed doctrine of providence. God governs all his creatures and all their actions, including a pagan emperor who does not know him. Cyrus acts freely for his own reasons, and God's purpose for his people is carried out through him.
nodes.is_servant_light: Reformed readers see here that God's saving purpose was never limited to one nation. The servant is given as a light for the nations, and Acts 13:47 shows the apostles treating that mission as their marching order. The church's preaching to the world is the servant's own work continued.
nodes.is_servant_obedient: Reformed theology speaks of Christ's willing obedience in his suffering. He was not overpowered. He gave his back. The New Testament does not cite this passage, so the tradition reads it of Christ by its place among the servant passages and by its likeness to the passion accounts.
nodes.is_servant_suffering: This chapter stands at the center of the Reformed doctrine of the atonement. The servant suffers in the place of others, bears their iniquities, and makes many to be accounted righteous. The Shorter Catechism's answer on Christ's humiliation prints Isaiah 53:3 and 53:10 among its proofs.
nodes.is_invitation: Reformed theology calls this the free offer of the gospel. God sincerely invites all who hear to come and receive what they cannot buy. The tradition holds this together with its teaching that God's word accomplishes what he purposes, as the same chapter says.
nodes.is_anointed: The Larger Catechism explains the name Christ by his anointing with the Holy Spirit to be prophet, priest, and king, and it prints Luke 4:18 and 21, where Jesus reads this passage, among its proofs. Here the anointed one speaks mostly as a prophet, bringing good news.
nodes.is_new_creation: The Reformed hope is larger than souls going to heaven. It is the resurrection of the body and a renewed creation where God lives with his people. The Standards teach the return of Christ, the resurrection, and the last judgment, and they leave room for different views on the order of events before the end.
nodes.isn_mt1: This is the incarnation. The Standards confess that the Son of God became man by being conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the virgin Mary, and Matthew 1:23 is among the proofs printed with Shorter Catechism 21.
nodes.isn_mt4: Reformed readers notice how Matthew reads the prophet. He does not hunt for hidden meanings. He sees Jesus go to the very region Isaiah named and says the promise has come true there. The light is a person who preaches repentance and the kingdom.
nodes.isn_lk4: The Larger Catechism cites this scene for the meaning of the title Christ. Jesus is the one anointed with the Spirit, and his first recorded sermon claims that anointing for himself. Reformed theology treats his prophetic office as beginning in his own preaching and continuing through his word.
nodes.isn_jn12: John teaches two things the Reformed tradition holds together. People are responsible for their unbelief, and God is sovereign over who sees. John also says Isaiah saw Christ's glory, which supports reading the Old Testament's visions of the LORD in the light of the Son.
nodes.isn_acts8: Reformed readers value this scene as a picture of how Scripture is understood. The Ethiopian has the text and needs a guide. Philip does not bring a different message. He begins with the passage in front of the man and preaches Jesus from it. Faith and baptism follow.
nodes.isn_1pet2: Peter holds together what the Reformed tradition insists on keeping together. Christ bore our sins as a substitute, and Christ is our example in suffering. The first is the ground of salvation. The second is the shape of the Christian life that flows from it.
nodes.isn_rev21: The Standards teach that Christ will return, the dead will be raised, and God will judge the world. This vision shows what lies beyond that day for his people: God dwelling with them in a creation made new. Reformed readers generally understand it as this creation renewed and not simply replaced, though the text does not settle every detail.
nodes.rv_christ: The Standards speak of Christ's exaltation: he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come to judge the world at the last day. This vision shows that exalted Christ, and it shows him among his churches. He is not absent while they wait for him.
nodes.rv_churches: Reformed teaching holds that Christ is the only head of the church and that he rules it by his word and Spirit. The seven letters show him doing so. He examines real congregations, with their mixture of truth and error, and calls them to repent. The tradition has always said that the purest churches on earth are subject to both mixture and error.
nodes.rv_throne: The Shorter Catechism says God's works of providence are his most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all his creatures and all their actions. Revelation 4 shows that in a picture. Reformed readers treat the throne as the fixed point of the whole book. Whatever follows happens under it.
nodes.rv_lamb: This chapter holds together Christ's two estates, humiliation and exaltation. He conquered by being slain, and he is now worshiped with the Father. The ransom is for people from every tribe and nation, and it does what it sets out to do: it makes them a kingdom and priests.
nodes.rv_seals: However the seals are placed in time, Reformed readers draw the same doctrine from them: war, scarcity, and death are not outside Christ's rule. The Lamb opens every seal. The martyrs' cry also teaches that God's justice is something his people may pray for and wait for.
nodes.rv_multitude: The Reformed doctrine of perseverance says that those whom God has called and sealed by his Spirit can never finally fall away. This chapter shows it. God's servants are sealed before the winds blow, and the same people stand before the throne at the end, their robes made white by the Lamb's blood and not by their own strength.
nodes.rv_trumpets: The trumpets are warnings, and they show both God's patience and the hardness of the human heart, which does not repent under judgment alone. Reformed theology concludes that repentance is a gift of God. The seventh trumpet states the confidence of the Standards, that Christ as king will conquer all his and our enemies.
nodes.rv_dragon: Confession 8.6 speaks of Christ as the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head. Reformed readers see that promise worked out here. The decisive battle is already won by the blood of the Lamb, and the church's present suffering is the anger of a defeated enemy.
nodes.rv_beasts: Reformed readers have applied this chapter in different ways. The lasting lesson is that when any earthly power demands the worship or final loyalty that belongs to God, Christians must refuse. The names of those who do not bow are written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (13:8), which is the ground of their endurance.
nodes.rv_babylon: Reformed readers take from this vision a warning against loving the world. Babylon is attractive and rich, and God's people are told to come out of her. However the city is identified, the Standards' teaching that Christ will judge the world in righteousness is pictured here ahead of time.
nodes.rv_supper: Reformed theology speaks of the union of Christ and his church, and Scripture's own picture of it is marriage. The Bride's linen is given to her, and it is also the righteous deeds of the saints. The tradition explains that the good works of believers are real and are also the fruit of grace. The Lord's Supper looks ahead to this meal.
nodes.rv_return: The Standards teach that Christ will come again at the last day in great power to judge the world. Most Reformed readers see that day here. Those who take the passage as Christ's conquest by the gospel in this age confess the same bodily return on the basis of other texts.
nodes.rv_millennium: The Westminster Standards teach a general resurrection of the just and the unjust and a last judgment at Christ's return, and they do not set out a doctrine of the thousand years. Reformed and Presbyterian churches have had amillennial, postmillennial, and historic premillennial ministers. The Standards' stress on one people of God in one covenant of grace is why dispensational schemes have not been received.
nodes.rv_judgment: The Confession's last chapter is on the last judgment. God has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ, and all persons who have lived on earth will appear before him. Reformed theology adds what the book of life shows: those who are acquitted are acquitted in Christ, and their works are evidence, not payment.
nodes.rv_new_creation: The Reformed hope is the resurrection of the body and life with God in a creation made new. The heart of it is the covenant promise that runs through all of Scripture, I will be their God and they shall be my people, here kept in full.
nodes.rv_river: Reformed theology reads the Bible as one story from the garden to the city. The tree of life, lost through Adam's sin, is given back through Christ, and the curse is removed. The closing invitation to take the water of life without price is among the Scripture proofs the Confession prints for the free offer of life in the covenant of grace.
nodes.rvo_daniel7: Daniel 7 is a main source for the Reformed doctrine of Christ's kingly office. The kingdom is given to the Son of Man by the Ancient of Days, it embraces all peoples, and it cannot be destroyed. Earthly empires are real and beastly, and they are temporary.
nodes.rvo_ezekiel1: Reformed readers take from Ezekiel 1 that God is present with and sovereign over his people wherever they are. The exiles had lost the temple. They had not lost God. His throne has wheels.
nodes.rvo_passover: Confession 7.5 names the paschal lamb among the types and ordinances by which the covenant of grace was administered under the law, all foresignifying Christ to come. It also teaches that these were sufficient for that time to build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah. The Passover was a real deliverance and a real means of grace as well as a picture of things to come.
nodes.rvo_zechariah4: This vision is a standard text for the Reformed conviction that the church is built by the Spirit of God through ordinary and unimpressive means. The day of small things is not to be despised. In Revelation the lampstands are congregations.
nodes.rvo_seed: In Reformed theology, Genesis 3:15 is the first gospel promise. Confession 8.6 identifies Christ as the seed of the woman who should bruise the serpent's head, and says the benefits of his redemption were given to the elect in all ages from the beginning of the world.
nodes.rvo_isaiah65: Reformed teaching holds that God's purpose in redemption is as wide as creation. The God who created the heavens and the earth will create them new. Grace does not abandon the world God made. It restores it.
nodes.rvo_ezekiel47: Reformed readers generally take Ezekiel's temple and river as prophecy in the forms of the old covenant, fulfilled in Christ and his Spirit and finally in the new creation, and not as a building still to be put up. Life flows from where God dwells, and in the end he dwells with his people.

paths.week1_seed: This week follows promises that Reformed theology reads within the one covenant of grace. Christ is their substance and fulfillment.
paths.week2_king: This week follows the promise of the king. The catechisms identify kingship as one of Christ's three offices.
paths.week3_sign: This week centers on the incarnation announced and fulfilled: the eternal Son took a true human nature and was born of Mary.
paths.week4_town: This week follows the promised ruler to the humble circumstances of his birth. The town's name is not itself a prophecy.
paths.christmas: Christmas is the incarnation and birth of the only redeemer, truly God and truly man in one person.
paths.deut_book: Walking Deuteronomy straight through puts a Reformed reader in front of the law as covenant preaching. God rescued a people, bound himself to them, told them how to live, and set blessing and curse in front of them. The Confession treats that whole arrangement as one administration of the covenant of grace, sufficient for its time and pointing to Christ. The book ends without the prophet it promised, which is where the second path begins.
paths.deut_nt: This path shows the apostles and Jesus himself reading Deuteronomy as a word that still speaks. Reformed theology accounts for that with one covenant under two administrations, which is the Confession's own language. The quotations are not proof texts pulled loose from their setting. Each one is used for something the Deuteronomy passage was already saying, with the one addition that the apostles make openly: that the promise and the curse and the near word all come to rest on Christ.
paths.isaiah_through: Read straight through, Isaiah moves from the holiness of God and the guilt of his people to a servant who bears that guilt and a creation made new. Reformed theology finds its main themes here in order: sin, judgment, a remnant kept by grace, a substitute, a free invitation, and a final renewal. The Confession says the covenant of grace was administered before Christ by promises and prophecies that pointed to him, and Isaiah is the fullest example.
paths.isaiah_nt: This path shows the apostles, and Jesus himself, reading Isaiah as a word about Christ. Reformed theology explains that with one covenant of grace under two administrations. The quotations are not pulled loose from their setting. Each uses Isaiah for something Isaiah was already saying, and adds what the apostles state openly, that it has come true in Jesus.
paths.rev_through: Reformed readers come to Revelation with humility about its details and confidence about its center. The Standards confess what the book shows most plainly: Christ is exalted and reigns, he will return to judge, the dead will be raised, and God will dwell with his people forever. On the questions the Standards leave open, such as the thousand years, Reformed churches have allowed differing views.
paths.rev_ot: This path shows why Reformed theology speaks of one covenant of grace and one story. John describes the end in words taken from Moses, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Zechariah, because the God who made those promises is the one who keeps them in Christ. The path also takes care over the difference between what the text states and what readers infer.
